reasoningSteps: Q01 assumptions: a closed, pure single qubit in computational order |0>, |1>; amplitudes a=√3/2 and b=1/2 are real and dimensionless. A state vector is not a histogram of hidden classical bits.
Normalize by the Hilbert-space inner product: |a|²+|b|²=(3/4)+(1/4)=1. Measurement probabilities follow the squared amplitude magnitudes, not their unsquared values.
An ideal Z-basis measurement has P(0)=0.75 and P(1)=0.25. Ten independent ideal shots have expected count 7.5 for outcome 0, not a guarantee of exactly 7 or 8.
Falsification: reporting P(0)=√3/2≈0.8660 would violate the Born rule; choosing a=b=1 without normalization gives probability total 2, not a valid state.
Offline derivation: compute squared magnitudes and assert |norm−1|<10^−12, P(0)=0.75, P(1)=0.25; compare a different relative phase while preserving Z probabilities.
Source and limitation: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/quantum/concepts-the-qubit; numerical probabilities describe an ideal isolated state, not calibrated hardware error rates.

reasoningSteps: Q02 model: ideal pure qubit initially |0>, exact H=1/√2[[1,1],[1,−1]] and Z=diag(1,−1). Matrices act right-to-left; amplitudes are dimensionless.
After the first H, the vector is |+>=[1,1]/√2; after Z, it is |->=[1,−1]/√2.
Applying H again gives HZH|0>=|1>, so ideal Z-basis probabilities are P(0)=0 and P(1)=1; equivalently HZH=X on this model.

Falsification: HZH is palindromic, so reversing this three-gate sequence cannot expose an order error. Under rightmost-first matrix action, HZ|0>=|+> means Z then H, while ZH|0>=|-> means H then Z; neither two-gate circuit yields |1>.
Independent invariant: multiply each gate's conjugate transpose by itself and check identity; verify the state norm remains 1 after every step.
Reference: https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/learning/en/courses/utility-scale-quantum-computing/bits-gates-and-circuits. This is a noiseless circuit-level identity, not an actual device fidelity claim.

reasoningSteps: Q03 model: a pure qubit |ψ>=√0.2|0>+√0.8|1>, measured repeatedly in computational basis with ideal independent state preparation.
The norm is 0.2+0.8=1, so P(0)=0.2, P(1)=0.8; an exactly known state does not imply a deterministic single-shot outcome.
For n=20 shots the binomial expectation of zero counts is np=4, with variance np(1−p)=3.2 and standard deviation √3.2≈1.788854 counts.
Falsification: asserting every batch of 20 shots must have exactly four zeros is false; even observing zero zeros has positive probability 0.8^20≈0.011529.
Offline exact oracle: compute probabilities, expectation, variance, and probability of no zeros, without generating or claiming measured samples.
Reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/quantum/concepts-the-qubit; actual measurement noise, readout calibration, and non-independent trials require separate modeling.

On the same state E(XX)=+1 but E(YY)=−1; a merely classical diagonal mixture of |00> and |11> reproduces ZZ while giving E(XX)=0.

reasoningSteps: Q05 model: ideal teleportation of |ψ>=|+> using a pre-shared Bell pair and two classical correction bits; Bob receives X^b Z^a|ψ> before correction, up to global phase.
Take the illustrative branch a=1,b=0: Bob's uncorrected state is Z|+>=|->=[1,−1]/√2, and Bob applies Z again to recover |+>.
The corrected state's overlap fidelity |<+|+>|²=1, while the uncorrected branch has |<+|−>|²=0. These are exact conditional branch values, not observed device success rates.
Falsification: the claim that a Bell pair alone instantly transmits |ψ> fails because Bob's corrective Pauli operation depends on two classical bits that must arrive.
Offline reproduction: apply Z twice to |+>, verify conditional branch fidelity 0 before correction and 1 afterward; other measurement branches use I,X,Z,or XZ.

advanced-no-cloning.essentialQuestion: Why would a single unitary that perfectly copies both |0> and |+> contradict the preservation of inner products?
advanced-no-cloning.verifiedBoundary: No universal physical operation can perfectly copy an arbitrary unknown quantum state.
advanced-no-cloning.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a workshop with specialized tools and workers. Some resources do different jobs and coordination matters. The real hardware, mathematics, or protocol is defined by the verified claim and evidence.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: Known states can be re-prepared; arbitrary unknown quantum states cannot be universally cloned.

reasoningSteps: Q06 assumptions: a hypothetical universal deterministic unitary U clones every unknown pure qubit using the same blank |0>; inner products of inputs must be preserved.
Choose |u>=|0> and |v>=|+>, whose overlap magnitude is |<u|v>|=1/√2≈0.70710678.
Two perfect copies would have overlap |<uu|vv>|=|<u|v>|²=1/2, contradicting unitarity because 1/√2 ≠ 1/2.
Falsification: cloning known orthogonal basis states with CNOT is possible and does not contradict the theorem; the impossibility is universal unknown-state cloning.
Offline oracle: compute the original overlap and would-be copy overlap and assert their difference exceeds 0.2; do not claim measurement or simulation establishes the full theorem.

Reference: https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/learning/en/courses/basics-of-quantum-information/quantum-circuits/limitations-on-quantum-information; a universal exact deterministic cloner would require s=s² for every input overlap s, impossible for nonorthogonal distinct states with 0<|s|<1. Approximate cloning and state estimation are different tasks.

reasoningSteps: Q07 model: the three-qubit repetition encoding α|000>+β|111> corrects at most one X (bit-flip) error; it is not a universal arbitrary-error code.
Inject X on the middle qubit: α|010>+β|101>; parity checks Z₀Z₁ and Z₁Z₂ both have eigenvalue −1, conventionally syndrome bit pair 11.
Apply X to that middle qubit again and recover α|000>+β|111>. For α=√0.3, β=√0.7, the output norm stays 1.
Falsification: a Z error on the middle qubit has syndrome 00 in these Z-parity checks, so this code does not diagnose phase errors.
Offline exercise: derive the four syndromes 00,10,11,01 for no X, X on first, second, third respectively under the stated check order.

Reference: https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/learning/en/courses/foundations-of-quantum-error-correction/correcting-quantum-errors/repetition-codes; no claim is made about fault tolerance, hardware correction threshold, or simultaneous multiple errors.

advanced-nisq.essentialQuestion: Under a toy model of independent 0.99 gate-survival events, how fast does whole-circuit survival fall from four gates to twelve, and why can that model not stand in for real device noise?
advanced-nisq.verifiedBoundary: NISQ describes quantum processors large enough to explore nontrivial circuits but still limited by noise, imperfect gates, and lack of full fault tolerance.

reasoningSteps: Q08 toy model: independent identical synthetic gate-survival events, each probability q=0.99; this is deliberately NOT a fitted quantum-device noise model.
A four-gate synthetic circuit has all-survive probability 0.99^4=0.96059601; twelve gates have 0.99^12≈0.8863848717.
Falsification: multiplying gate survival probabilities is unjustified for correlated, coherent, leakage, crosstalk, or state-dependent errors; a real benchmark must establish its own model.
Reproducible algebra: verify q^4 and q^12 and their ratio q^8; contrast a hypothetical perfect gate q=1 whose all-survive probability is 1 at any depth.
Interpretation: increasing gate count raises accumulated failure exposure under this explicitly independent toy assumption, but does not quantify device error-corrected logical success.
Reference: https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/learning/en/courses/utility-scale-quantum-computing/bits-gates-and-circuits; these probabilities are synthetic assumptions, never measured QPU performance.

advanced-quantum-circuit-depth.essentialQuestion: Why does the circuit H(q0), X(q1), CNOT(q0→q1), Z(q0) contain four gates but have an ideal depth of three?
advanced-quantum-circuit-depth.verifiedBoundary: Circuit depth measures how many sequential layers of operations are required when gates that act on disjoint qubits can run in parallel.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: Gate count measures amount of work; depth measures sequential dependency along the critical quantum path.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: Four independent single-qubit gates can occupy one parallel layer, while four dependent gates on the same qubit require multiple layers. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.

reasoningSteps: Q09 assumptions: an abstract two-qubit ideal circuit with H(q0) and X(q1) first, then CNOT(q0→q1), then Z(q0); disjoint-qubit gates may be concurrent.
H(q0) and X(q1) form layer 1; CNOT uses both qubits and must be layer 2; Z(q0) follows CNOT and is layer 3. Gate count is four but ideal layer depth is three.
Falsification: simply setting depth equal to number of gates gives 4 instead of 3; assigning CNOT to layer 1 would conflict with both earlier gates.
An offline dependency-list scheduler verifies depth=max(dependency-layer+1)=3 for this partial order; adding Z(q1) after CNOT may share layer 3 with Z(q0).
Hardware scheduling caveat: gate durations, connectivity, routing, classical dependencies, and hardware-native decompositions may change physical execution time.
Reference: https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/learning/en/courses/quantum-computing-in-practice/running-quantum-circuits; this is logical circuit depth, not measured wall-clock latency.

Place H0 and X1 in layer 1, CNOT01 in layer 2, and Z0 in layer 3.

reasoningSteps: Q10 model: normalized single pure state |ψ>=cos(θ/2)|0>+e^{iφ}sin(θ/2)|1>, using radians; this describes an ideal qubit modulo global phase.
For θ=π/2 and φ=π/2, the Bloch vector is (sinθ cosφ,sinθ sinφ,cosθ)=(0,1,0), within floating-point rounding.
Therefore ideal P(Y+)=1, P(X+)=0.5 and P(Z+)=0.5 by P(axis+)= (1+r_axis)/2.
Falsification: using degrees directly in standard JavaScript Math.sin for θ=90 incorrectly treats 90 as radians; a general mixed state also lies inside rather than on the pure-state sphere.
Compute the three components and assert squared vector length 1 and all indicated basis probabilities without shot sampling.
Reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/quantum/concepts-the-qubit; readout basis rotations and device calibration are outside the pure-state model.

reasoningSteps: Q11 assumptions: ideal H=(1/√2)[[1,1],[1,−1]], computational basis [|0>,|1>], exact coherent gates and dimensionless amplitudes.
Apply H to |1>=[0,1] to obtain |->=[1/√2,−1/√2], with equal Z-basis probabilities 0.5 and 0.5.
A second H returns |1>: H²=I, not H. In particular H|->=|1> follows by explicit matrix multiplication.
Falsification: treating H as random irreversible coin tossing predicts loss of relative phase and would not explain deterministic H² recovery.
Offline matrix checks: HᵀH=I and H²|1>=[0,1], with every vector normalized.
Reference: https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/learning/en/courses/utility-scale-quantum-computing/bits-gates-and-circuits; no classical sample generator substitutes for coherent amplitudes.

reasoningSteps: Q12 model: |ψ>=0.6|0>+0.8|1> is normalized (0.36+0.64=1); ideal X swaps its basis amplitudes.

Falsification: interpreting X as a universal classical NOT of every measurement basis fails: X|+>=|+> and no Z-basis measurement probabilities change for |+>.
Compare X|ψ> and X²|ψ>=|ψ>; the X matrix is its own inverse and its own conjugate transpose.

reasoningSteps: Q13 ideal model: first qubit is control, second target, computational basis order |00>,|01>,|10>,|11>; CNOT flips the target only in the control=1 component.

Probabilities are P(00)=P(11)=0.5, P(01)=P(10)=0; changing the control input to |0> leaves target |0> unchanged.
Falsification: flipping the target unconditionally would map |00> to |01> and cannot represent CNOT; applying a gate independently to the control and target cannot create this Bell entanglement.

reasoningSteps: Q14 model: normalized qubit |ψ>=√0.6|0>+i√0.4|1>; multiply the ENTIRE vector by e^{iπ/2}=i, not just one amplitude.

Independent invariant: both state vectors have norm 1 and |<ψ|iψ>|²=1, despite their distinct coordinate entries.
Offline arrays of complex pairs can check each amplitude and probability; no finite-shot sampling is needed.
Reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/quantum/concepts-the-qubit; phase observability depends on relative phases and comparison context, not absolute phase of an isolated state.
